summary:
Astro Explorers is a free browser-based game where children and teenagers manage a research base on Mars and make decisions under pressure. Each player guides their astronaut to different areas of the base (greenhouse, oxygen plant, power station, laboratory, and shelter) and plays short minigames to keep the crew alive: growing crops through hydroponics, producing oxygen using technology like NASA's MOXIE, cleaning solar panels, and protecting the crew from solar storms. Each minigame ends with a real NASA science fact, making learning part of the fun.
Players can explore on their own or team up with friends by sharing a link. Each player controls their own astronaut, and helping others earns stars. The difficulty increases over time, and every setback makes survival more challenging, so teamwork truly matters.
We created Astro Explorers for classrooms in Santiago del Estero, Argentina. It runs in both Spanish and English, works on computers with just 4 GB of RAM and mobile phones, and requires no installation or personal information. It also includes a teacher's guide. The game turns space weather, radiation, and life support into real decisions students make for themselves, showing why NASA's research matters for life on Mars and here on Earth.

What it does and how it works

Astro Explorers is a browser game where players run a research base on Mars. Each player controls one astronaut and walks them to the places of the base: greenhouse, kitchen, oxygen plant, power room, lab, airlock, shelter, workshop, dunes and ice pits. Arriving at a place opens a short mini-game, and the result helps the crew. Players grow crops with hydroponics, make oxygen with electrolysis like NASA's MOXIE, fix solar circuits, balance equations in the lab, mine materials and build new modules. Meanwhile, events such as solar storms, dust storms and failures force quick decisions, and players must take cover in the shelter during radiation peaks. Every mini-game ends with a short NASA fact. The game starts easy and gets harder over time. Each astronaut lost makes survival harder.

Benefits and intended impact

Students learn space weather, radiation, life support and energy by making decisions, not by memorizing. Multiplayer is simple: one player shares a link, and friends join with a nickname from any phone or computer, even on the same school Wi-Fi. Helping a teammate earns stars and makes their task worth more, so cooperation is part of the game. A Spanish teacher guide explains each system and how to use the game in class. We want students in Santiago del Estero, Argentina, and other places with few resources, to feel that space science is something they can understand and take part in.

Tools and technologies

- TypeScript, React 19 and Phaser 3 (an isometric map of the base and the Martian surface), built with Vite.

- A deterministic simulation engine: fixed time steps and a seeded random generator. Every player action is recorded as a command, so games can be replayed exactly and the ranking is fair.

- A small Node.js relay server for multiplayer. The host's browser runs the game, and the server only passes messages.

- Vitest automated tests, including a bot that plays full games to check balance.

- NASA educational material ("Living on Mars" teacher guide, MOXIE, Perseverance and space weather sources) for the facts.

- Claude Code (AI coding assistant) to help write code and documentation. The team reviewed and tested every change.

- No special hardware: it runs on regular laptops and phones.

Creativity

The game is a full base you explore, not a quiz. Science is part of the mechanics: hiding from radiation, keeping dust off solar panels and making oxygen from CO₂ are actions that save your crew. Each place has its own themed mini-game, and helping others is rewarded with points.

Factors we considered

- Young players: no personal data, only nicknames, and no violent language.

- Low-cost hardware: a light mode, optimized drawing and less network traffic, so it runs on 4 GB machines.

- Language: English by default, with Spanish available.

- Accessibility: icons and very little text, reduced motion, and full screen on phones.

- Scientific honesty: we mark which numbers are gameplay simplifications and which are NASA data.

- Teamwork in the code: a code policy lets team members add mini-games without breaking the main game.
